summary: This informational RFC was published on April 1 and is humorous. It claims to define the Null Packet, which earlier RFCs mentioned many times without defining it. It should not be taken as a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st RFC jokes about a packet that contains nothing. It claims the packet is formally defined while leaving its definition blank.

questions: what is the null packet in rfc 6592
why is the null packet definition blank
subtitle: An April 1st joke that defines a packet containing nothing at all.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke claims to correct the omission of a formal definition for the often-mentioned Null Packet.
tldr.mechanism: It calls the Null Packet zero-dimensional and says it cannot have a protocol identifier; its formal-definition section is left blank.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a humor document, not a usable packet specification.

today: RFC 6592 is an Informational April 1st joke about the Null Packet. Its formal-definition section is intentionally blank.

sections.title: The Elusive Null Packet
sections.content:
The memo says Null Packets have been mentioned in earlier RFCs without an explicit definition. It explains that “nothing” in a header-compression discussion means an explicit lack of response, not a packet compressed until it disappears.

It argues that a Null Packet cannot have a protocol identifier because assigning it a value would contradict its null nature. It says even numeric zero is excluded, while the empty string is not.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC treats “nothing is returned” as a packet with no contents. The joke says giving that packet an identifier would make it no longer null.

sections.title: A Zero-Dimensional Packet
sections.content:
The memo calls the Null Packet a zero-dimensional packet and says it exists because it can be defined without contradiction. Its Formal Definition section is intentionally left blank.

It distinguishes the Null Packet from an imaginary packet and from the null device, which discards packets. These distinctions are part of the RFC's wordplay.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC calls the packet zero-dimensional but leaves its formal definition empty. It jokes about confusing this idea with imaginary packets or a null device.

sections.title: Performance and Security Jokes
sections.content:
The RFC says that sending more Null Packets does not increase their bit rate, which remains zero. It suggests that ordinary traffic metrics cannot measure such traffic usefully.

The security section jokes about firewalls, the Evil Bit, and denial of denial of service. It asks IANA not to create an empty registry for the Null Packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke says sending more empty packets still sends zero bits. Its security and registry sections extend the wordplay.
